displayQuote: I do not believe in using women in combat, because females are too fierce

meta.title: Who really said "I do not believe in using women in combat, because females are too fierce"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Attributed to Margaret Mead, but cited only to a 1977 quote anthology. Her sourced 1968 draft remarks say something close, and mean the opposite of the meme.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I do not believe in using women in combat, because females are too fierce'?
meta.ogDescription: Mead's one-liner is documented only in a 1977 quote anthology. Her sourced 1968 remarks argue women might be too fierce for the rules that limit war.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Mead, and consistent with a position she demonstrably held — but the polished one-liner is cited only as it appears in a 1977 quotation anthology, not in anything Mead is known to have written. The closest primary text anyone has produced is her own “Remarks about the Military Draft” (June 1968), collected in Margaret Mead, Some Personal Views (1979), which looks back on having said that women in combat “might be too fierce.”

source.heading: The closest thing to a source

docMeta.dd: “Remarks about the Military Draft,” June 1968 — collected 1979, ed. Rhoda Métraux, pp. 35–36 (Walker, New York)
As quoted in Quote Unquote (1977), comp. Lloyd Cory, p. 364 — a quotation anthology, not a Mead work
Not pinned to any Mead original

source.excerpt: Women should be permitted to volunteer for non-combat service… the evidence of history and comparative studies of other species suggest that women as a fighting body might be far less amenable to the rules that prevent war from becoming a massacre… That is what I meant by saying that women in combat might be too fierce.
trail: Wikiquote’s Margaret Mead page ↗ gives the exact one-liner a single citation: “As quoted in Quote Unquote (1977) by Lloyd Cory, p. 364.” That is a compiled quotation anthology, so it establishes that the sentence was in circulation under Mead’s name in 1977 — not where she said it.

The same page carries a much longer statement in its 1960s section, sourced to “Remarks about the Military Draft” (June 1968), in Margaret Mead, Some Personal Views (1979), ed. Rhoda Metraux, pp. 35–36 ↗, ending: “That is what I meant by saying that women in combat might be too fierce.”

Open Library’s record for that 1979 volume ↗ (Walker, New York; 286 pp.) notes that the questions and answers it gathers were first published in Redbook from 1963 to January 1979 — a run the June 1968 date falls inside.
The version people actually share has no citation at all: Goodreads lists it with tags and no source ↗, under its standing notice that community quotes are unverified.
source.excerptNote: This is the longer, primary-sourced statement — not the circulating one-liner. Ellipses mark omitted text; Wikiquote’s own transcription also carries a bracketed cut after “non-combat service.” Note the last sentence: Mead is looking back on a remark she had already made, which is why the compact version feels authentic even though no one has produced its original.

Since no pre-1931 publication of this wording exists, treat the sentence as in-copyright: quote it briefly, with attribution.

author.name: Margaret Mead
author.heading: Who was Margaret Mead?
author.metaLine: 1901–1978 · American cultural anthropologist, museum curator and magazine columnist
author.bio: Margaret Mead was an American cultural anthropologist who became, in the anthropologist Paul Shankman’s phrase, anthropology’s most significant public voice of the twentieth century. She spent most of her career at the American Museum of Natural History — assistant curator from 1926, curator of ethnology from 1946 to 1969 — while teaching at Columbia, Fordham and the University of Rhode Island. From the 1960s she also wrote a monthly Redbook column with Rhoda Métraux, which is where most of her short, quotable public pronouncements come from, and which is why so many “Mead quotes” circulate today with no book attached to them.

copyAttribution: "I do not believe in using women in combat, because females are too fierce." — attributed to Margaret Mead (1901–1978). Widely credited to Mead but not pinned to any of her own writings; documented as quoted in Lloyd Cory, comp., Quote Unquote (1977), p. 364. Mead's own "Remarks about the Military Draft" (June 1968), in Margaret Mead, Some Personal Views, ed. Rhoda Métraux (New York: Walker, 1979), 35–36, does say: "That is what I meant by saying that women in combat might be too fierce." Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Nobody stole this one — but it still travels wrong
misattribution.intro: No rival author is claiming this sentence. The problems are subtler: it circulates with no source at all, and it is quoted to mean roughly the opposite of what Mead argued.

items.why: The big aggregators print the line bare. Goodreads gives no book, no date and no source ↗, adding its standard note that community-submitted quotes are not verified; LibQuotes lists it — and the longer 1968 statement — with no citation either ↗.

Passed around as a compliment, it reads as praise for female ferocity. Mead’s documented argument runs the other way: women as a fighting body might be “far less amenable to the rules that prevent war from becoming a massacre” ↗ — a reason to keep them out of combat, not a tribute.

misattribution.truthLine: Mead really did say something very close to this — her own June 1968 remarks look back on “saying that women in combat might be too fierce” — but the polished one-liner is documented only as quoted in a 1977 quotation anthology ↗, never in a Mead text anyone has produced.

context.heading: What Mead was actually arguing
lead: Mead was the best-known anthropologist in America — the anthropologist Paul Shankman calls her anthropology’s most significant public voice of the twentieth century ↗ — and by the late 1960s she was also answering readers’ questions every month in Redbook alongside Rhoda Métraux. The military draft was the argument of the moment, and her documented position was that women should be able to volunteer for non-combat service.

The reasoning is the part the meme drops. Mead was not paying women a compliment. Her June 1968 remarks argue that a fighting body of women might be far less bound by the restraints that stop a war from becoming a massacre — a line of thought she had been circling since the introduction to Male and Female (1949), where she observed that female animals defending their young are “notoriously ferocious” and lack the mock-combat playfulness of males (both passages on Wikiquote ↗).
context.detailsSummary: Why the slogan and the sourced passage are not the same claim
detailsBody: The sourced 1968 passage is conditional and hedged: women as a fighting body might be less amenable to the rules that limit war, and Mead concedes there is no real way of knowing whether training that teaches men courage and restraint would work the same way for women. The circulating one-liner strips out the conditional and the caveat and leaves a flat declaration.

It also strips out the policy Mead was actually defending — that women should be admitted to national service in non-combat roles. Read whole, the passage is an argument for including women in the system; read as a slogan, it reads as an argument for keeping them out of it.
context.pull: That is what I meant by saying that women in combat might be too fierce.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Margaret Mead page contains "I do not believe in using women in combat, because females are too fierce" cited only as "As quoted in Quote Unquote (1977) by Lloyd Cory, p. 364", listed in the page's chronological "1970s" section beside other lines taken from 1974-1977 sources (Redbook April 1974, Newsweek 1976, Family Circle July 1977, Quotations for Our Time 1977) and not under any Mead book subsection; the same page carries the longer June 1968 "Remarks about the Military Draft" passage sourced to Margaret Mead, Some Personal Views (1979), ed. Rhoda Metraux, pp. 35-36, ending "That is what I meant by saying that women in combat might be too fierce", and a Male and Female (1949) Introduction line about female animals being "notoriously ferocious".

Open Library's work record shows "Margaret Mead, some personal views" by Margaret Mead and Rhoda Bubendey Metraux, published 1979 by Walker in New York, 286 pages, with an edition note that the questions and answers were first published in Redbook magazine from 1963 to January 1979.

Goodreads hosts the quote "I do not believe in using women in combat, because females are too fierce" attributed to Margaret Mead with no book, source or date cited, tagged combat/war/women, under Goodreads' notice that community-added quotes are not verified.
LibQuotes' Margaret Mead women page lists both the one-liner and the longer "Women should be permitted to volunteer for non-combat service" statement, neither with a cited source.

Wikipedia records Margaret Mead as an American cultural anthropologist born 16 December 1901 and died 15 November 1978, described by the anthropologist Paul Shankman as "anthropology's most significant public voice during the twentieth century", curator at the American Museum of Natural History (assistant curator 1926, curator of ethnology 1946-1969), and author of a monthly Redbook column co-authored with Rhoda Metraux.
Wikipedia records Male and Female: A Study of the Sexes in a Changing World as a 1949 book by Margaret Mead published by William Morrow and Company.
